summary: Specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms that can be implemented by IPv6 hosts and routers, helping the move from the old address system to the new one. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4213.

plainLanguage.summary: Moving from old addresses to new ones takes time. This describes tricks so both kinds of computers can work together while that happens.

questions: what is ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling
what is a dual stack node
what is an ipv4 compatible ipv6 address
subtitle: How IPv6 nodes stay compatible with IPv4 by running both stacks or tunneling IPv6 inside IPv4.

tldr.problem: IPv6 had to be deployed on top of a huge installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers, and the IPv6 routing infrastructure would only be built up over time.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 nodes can implement both protocols (dual IP layer) and can wrap IPv6 packets in IPv4 headers, using either configured tunnels or automatic tunnels built on IPv4-compatible addresses.
tldr.outcome: It gave implementers a transition toolbox, but the RFC was obsoleted by RFC 4213.

today: RFC 2893 was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 1933 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4213, so it is no longer the current specification.

sections.title: The Transition Toolbox
sections.content:
The RFC starts from one idea: a successful IPv6 transition depends on compatibility with the large installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers. It expects that most nodes will need such compatibility for a long time, and perhaps indefinitely. IPv6 nodes built for environments where IPv4 interoperability is not needed do not have to implement these mechanisms.

Four mechanisms are defined: a dual IP layer, configured tunneling of IPv6 over IPv4, IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses, and automatic tunneling. They are described as a "transition toolbox": sites and implementations pick what they need, and the RFC expects other tools to be specified in later documents.

An IPv4-only node implements only IPv4. An IPv6/IPv4 node implements both. An IPv6-only node implements only IPv6, and its operation is not addressed here.

An IPv4-compatible IPv6 address has an all-zeros high-order 96-bit prefix and an IPv4 address in the low-order 32 bits. Any other IPv6 address is an IPv6-native address. In configured tunneling the IPv4 tunnel endpoint comes from configuration on the encapsulating node. In automatic tunneling it is taken from the IPv4 address embedded in the packet's IPv4-compatible destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a toolbox of tricks for living with two kinds of addresses at once. You only pick up the tools you need.

sections.title: Dual IP Layer and DNS
sections.content:
The simplest way to stay compatible is for a node to carry a complete IPv4 and IPv6 implementation. Such a node can talk IPv4 to IPv4 nodes and IPv6 to IPv6 nodes. It can run with only IPv4 enabled, only IPv6 enabled, or both, and MAY offer a configuration switch to turn either stack off. It uses IPv4 mechanisms such as DHCP for its IPv4 addresses and IPv6 mechanisms such as stateless address autoconfiguration for its IPv6-native addresses.

For DNS, resolver libraries on these nodes MUST handle both A records and A6/AAAA records. When a name has both kinds, the resolver MAY return only the IPv6 address, only the IPv4 address, or both, and MAY order them to influence which IP version applications prefer. An implementation MUST let the application control whether such filtering takes place.

The RFC recommends not publishing A6/AAAA records for a node until the address is assigned, configured, and the interface is on a link connected to the IPv6 infrastructure. Otherwise an isolated node may try IPv6 to a peer, fail, and wait a few minutes for TCP to time out before falling back to IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer that speaks both languages can chat with anyone. But do not list your new-language phone number until it really works, or friends will keep calling a dead line first.

sections.title: How Tunneling Works
sections.content:
Tunneling carries IPv6 across IPv4 routing infrastructure by wrapping each IPv6 packet in an IPv4 header. Tunnels can run router-to-router, host-to-router, host-to-host or router-to-host. The entry node builds the IPv4 header; the exit node reassembles if needed, removes the IPv4 header and processes the IPv6 packet.

The encapsulating IPv4 header uses version 4, header length 5 (no options), protocol 41, a source address that is the encapsulating node's outgoing interface, and the tunnel endpoint as destination. The IPv6 hop limit is decremented by 1 across the tunnel, so the tunnel acts as a single hop and is hidden from tools like traceroute. A decapsulating node MUST be able to reassemble an IPv4 packet of 1300 bytes.

For size, the encapsulating node can track the IPv4 path MTU and treat the tunnel as a link whose MTU is that value minus 20 bytes. Since every IPv6 link must have an MTU of at least 1280 bytes, a tunnel never advertises less than that. When the path allows it, the node sets the Don't Fragment flag and returns an IPv6 ICMP packet-too-big error for oversized packets.

Tunnel interfaces MUST have link-local addresses, formed from FE80::/64 plus an interface identifier made of the 32-bit IPv4 address padded with zeros on the left.
sections.plainLanguage: You put your new-style letter in an old-style envelope, mail it across the old post system, and the person at the far end opens the envelope and reads the letter.

sections.title: Configured Tunneling
sections.content:
In configured tunneling the encapsulating node stores the tunnel endpoint address for each tunnel and uses it as the destination of the IPv4 header. Which packets enter a tunnel is normally decided by the IPv6 routing table.

A host on a link with no IPv6 router MAY use a default configured tunnel: an IPv6 default route that points through a tunnel to an IPv6/IPv4 router at the edge of the IPv6 backbone. The endpoint can also be an IPv4 "anycast address" shared by several border routers, so traffic goes to the closest one and fails over if one goes down. To avoid fragments reaching different routers, the RFC suggests avoiding fragmentation (an IPv4 MTU of at least 1300 bytes) or avoiding frequent IPv4 routing changes.

The decapsulating node MUST check that the tunnel source is acceptable before forwarding. For bidirectional tunnels the source must be the other end of the tunnel. For unidirectional tunnels the node MUST have a configured list of acceptable IPv4 source prefixes, which defaults to empty.
sections.plainLanguage: A configured tunnel is a private road between two places that someone built on purpose. Your computer simply remembers where the road ends.

sections.title: Automatic Tunneling and IPv4-Compatible Addresses
sections.content:
An IPv4-compatible address is the 96-bit prefix 0:0:0:0:0:0 followed by an IPv4 address. A node acquires one by getting its IPv4 address in any normal way (DHCP, BOOTP, RARP or manual configuration) and prepending the prefix. A node SHOULD have such an address only if it is ready to accept IPv6 packets tunneled to that embedded IPv4 address.

When the IPv6 destination is IPv4-compatible, the tunnel endpoint is simply the low-order 32 bits of that address, so no tunnel needs configuring. An implementation can route the prefix 0:0:0:0:0:0/96 to a pseudo-interface that does this. The module MUST NOT send to IPv4 broadcast or multicast destinations and MUST drop packets whose embedded address is broadcast, multicast, 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1.

Isolated hosts often combine both techniques: automatic tunneling for IPv4-compatible destinations and a default configured tunnel for IPv6-native ones. For source address selection the RFC recommends using the IPv4-compatible source when the destination is IPv4-compatible, and the IPv6-native source when the destination is IPv6-native, so return traffic is symmetric.
sections.plainLanguage: The old-style address is tucked inside the new-style address like a note in a pocket. The sender just reads the note to know where to send the envelope.

sections.title: Security and Ingress Filtering
sections.content:
The RFC says tunneling is not known to introduce security holes except for the possibility of circumventing ingress filtering. To prevent that, a decapsulated packet MUST NOT be forwarded unless the node is explicitly configured to accept encapsulated packets from that IPv4 source.

Decapsulating nodes SHOULD silently discard packets with invalid IPv4 or IPv6 source addresses, such as multicast, broadcast, 0.0.0.0 and 127.0.0.1. Because an automatic tunnel always ends at the destination, any packet received over one SHOULD NOT be forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The person opening the envelope must not blindly pass the letter along to strangers. They only forward mail from senders they were told to trust.
